title: Cause and consequence
job: Why things happen and what follows, across a paragraph
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: ya que, puesto que and dado que take a whole CLAUSE — a subject and a verb — and they prefer the FRONT: Ya que no hay tren, vamos en coche. They are the words that let a cause be said first.
así que and por eso also take a clause, but they stand only AFTER the cause and open the CONSEQUENCE. Nothing may be fronted with them: No hay tren, así que vamos en coche, never the other way round.

por, gracias a, por culpa de and debido a take a NOUN and never a clause. Por la lluvia, no salimos — and never por llueve. This is the same por L3-M2 taught on work and pay, extended into cause, not a second word.

English because covers every job here and sits happily at either end. Spanish porque only FOLLOWS, so a fronted cause needs ya que instead. porque and por eso are L1-M9's and are re-used here, not re-opened.

sin embargo and por lo tanto are the careful, written pair — however and therefore. The everyday twins are pero and así que, which the course already owns, and a spoken paragraph reaches for those first.

sentences.display: No hay tren, así que vamos en coche.
sentences.cue: There's no train, so we're going by car.

words.note: Takes a whole clause and stands only after the cause. It opens the consequence, which is why nothing can be put in front of it.
The service, not one carriage. hay tren means there is a service running at all.
The word in Spain; carro and auto are the Latin American ones. en coche, by car, with no article.

sentences.trap: English so and Spanish así que line up almost exactly, which is the one free gift in this module — and it is why a learner uses así que for everything and never reaches for the front-loading connectors.
sentences.sound: a-SÍ ke, two words but one beat in speech; the í carries the stress and the qu is a plain k.

variations.display: No hay autobús, así que vamos en coche.
variations.cue: There's no bus, so we're going by car.

variations.display: No hay tren, así que hoy no salimos.
variations.cue: There's no train, so we're not going out today.

mistake.display: Así que no hay tren, vamos en coche.
mistake.why: así que only ever follows the cause. Fronted, the sentence needs ya que.

sentences.usage: Two friends deciding how to travel. The scene is tú, but the sentence carries no pronoun and works unchanged with usted.

sentences.display: Ya que no hay tren, vamos en coche.
sentences.cue: Since there's no train, we're going by car.

words.note: Takes a whole clause and prefers the FRONT — this is the word Spanish uses where English fronts because. Indexed whole: bare ya is L3-M10's already.

sentences.trap: English because goes at either end, so a learner writes Porque no hay tren, vamos en coche. It is understood and it is wrong: porque only follows, and the fronted cause is ya que.
sentences.sound: ya ke — the y is the soft j of yes at the start of a word, and the que is a plain ke.

variations.display: Ya que hay huelga, vamos en coche.
variations.cue: Since there's a strike, we're going by car.

variations.display: Ya que no tengo coche, voy en autobús.
variations.cue: Since I don't have a car, I'm going by bus.

mistake.display: Porque no hay tren, vamos en coche.
mistake.why: porque cannot open a sentence in ordinary Spanish. The fronted cause takes ya que.

sentences.usage: The same decision as S01 said the other way round — cause first. Neutral in both addresses; the scene here is tú.
sentences.mnemonic: Cause first means ya que; cause second means porque.

sentences.display: Hoy llueve mucho. Por eso no salimos de casa.
sentences.cue: It's raining a lot today. That's why we're not going out.

words.note: The we-form of salir. L3-M10 owns the infinitive salir; this is the cell the consequence needed.

sentences.trap: por eso is L1-M9's and is being re-used, not re-taught: it opens the consequence, the same job as así que, and the only difference is that por eso starts a new sentence while así que stays inside one.
sentences.sound: sa-LI-mos, stress on the li. LLUE-ve, and the ll is the y of yes.

variations.display: Hoy hay huelga. Por eso no salimos de casa.
variations.cue: There's a strike today. That's why we're not going out.

variations.display: Hoy llueve mucho. Por eso vamos en coche.
variations.cue: It's raining a lot today. That's why we're going by car.

mistake.display: Por eso hoy llueve mucho, no salimos.
mistake.why: por eso opens the CONSEQUENCE. Put in front of the cause it says the rain is the result, which is the opposite claim.

sentences.usage: Explaining a plan that changed, to anyone. Neutral, and the two short sentences are what make it a paragraph rather than a clause.
sentences.mnemonic: por eso points forward at the result.

sentences.display: Por la lluvia, no salimos de casa.
sentences.cue: Because of the rain, we're not going out.

words.note: The NOUN, which is what por needs. The verb llueve, L3-M4's, cannot follow por at all — that is the whole point of this row.

sentences.trap: English because of is two words and looks like a conjunction, so a learner puts a clause behind it. Spanish por is a preposition: a noun follows, never a verb.
sentences.sound: LLU-via, two syllables, and the ll is the y of yes.

variations.display: Por la lluvia, hoy no hay autobús.
variations.cue: Because of the rain, there's no bus today.

variations.display: Por la huelga, no salimos de casa.
variations.cue: Because of the strike, we're not going out.

mistake.display: Por llueve, no salimos de casa.
mistake.why: por takes a noun. The rain as a cause is por la lluvia; the verb needs ya que llueve.

sentences.usage: The reason given at the door, in one phrase. Neutral, and it is the shortest cause the module teaches.
sentences.mnemonic: por is a preposition, so a noun comes next.

sentences.display: Por culpa de la huelga, hoy no hay tren.
sentences.cue: Because of the strike, there's no train today.

words.note: por with the blame showing: the cause is something you resent. It takes a noun, exactly as por does, and it is three words that behave as one preposition.
A work stoppage. Spain talks about them often enough that this is everyday news vocabulary, not political vocabulary.

sentences.trap: por culpa de and gracias a are the same shape with opposite feeling — blame against credit. English has no neat pair, which is why a learner uses plain because of for both and sounds flat.
sentences.sound: por CUL-pa de, run together in one phrase; the de is barely there.

variations.display: Por culpa de la lluvia, hoy no salimos.
variations.cue: Because of the rain, we're not going out today.

variations.display: Por culpa de las obras, el tren tiene retraso.
variations.cue: Because of the roadworks, the train is delayed.

mistake.display: Por culpa de hay huelga, no hay tren.
mistake.why: por culpa de takes a noun like every por does: por culpa de la huelga.

sentences.usage: Complaining about something that went wrong, to anyone. Neutral, and the blame is in the phrase rather than the tone.
sentences.mnemonic: culpa is blame, so por culpa de is the bad news half.

sentences.display: Gracias a tu ayuda, ahora está todo listo.
sentences.cue: Thanks to your help, everything's ready now.

words.note: The credit half of the pair, and it takes a NOUN like the rest of them. The a never drops — gracias tu ayuda is not Spanish.

sentences.trap: English thanks to can be sarcastic — thanks to you, we missed it. Spanish gracias a is sincere, and the resentful version is por culpa de. Choosing the wrong one says the wrong thing.
sentences.sound: GRA-cias a, and in Spain the c of gracias is the th of think.

variations.display: Gracias a mi hermana, ahora está todo listo.
variations.cue: Thanks to my sister, everything's ready now.

variations.display: Gracias a tu ayuda, hoy salimos temprano.
variations.cue: Thanks to your help, we're leaving early today.

mistake.display: Gracias tu ayuda, ahora está todo listo.
mistake.why: gracias a is two words and the a is part of the connector, not an extra.

sentences.usage: Thanking someone for what their help made possible. The scene here is tú; the same phrase is unchanged with su ayuda for usted.
sentences.mnemonic: Credit takes gracias a, blame takes por culpa de.

sentences.display: Puesto que hay obras, el autobús tiene retraso.
sentences.cue: Since there are roadworks, the bus is delayed.

words.note: ya que's more careful twin: same job, same front position, a written or considered register. Takes a whole clause.
Always plural in this sense. hay obras is what a sign says when a street is dug up.
A noun. tener retraso is how a service is late; a person who is late uses llegar tarde instead.

sentences.trap: English since does double duty for time and cause, and a learner assumes puesto que does too. It does not: it is causal only, and the time since is desde.
sentences.sound: PUES-to ke, and the ue is one glide. re-TRA-so, stress on the tra.

variations.display: Puesto que hay huelga, no hay tren.
variations.cue: Since there's a strike, there's no train.

variations.display: Puesto que llueve mucho, vamos en coche.
variations.cue: Since it's raining a lot, we're going by car.
variations.changed: the cause, and a verb rather than hay

mistake.display: Puesto que obras, el autobús tiene retraso.
mistake.why: puesto que takes a whole clause, so the verb has to be there: puesto que hay obras.

sentences.usage: An announcement, or someone explaining a delay carefully. Neutral leaning formal — spoken Spanish would say como or ya que here.
sentences.mnemonic: puesto que is ya que in its good clothes.

sentences.display: Dado que no tengo tiempo, hoy como en casa.
sentences.cue: Given that I don't have time, today I'm eating at home.

words.note: The third front-loading connector, and the most written of the three. Same rule: a whole clause behind it, and the que is not optional.

sentences.trap: Sentence-initial como is the commonest way a Spaniard says this, and this module refuses it: como is already L1-M4's I eat, and a learner tapping it would be shown a note about eating — which this very sentence proves, since its main clause is that como.
sentences.sound: DA-do ke, and the d between vowels is soft, like the th of this.

variations.display: Dado que hay obras, vamos en autobús.
variations.cue: Given that there are roadworks, we're going by bus.

variations.display: Dado que no tengo coche, voy en tren.
variations.cue: Given that I don't have a car, I'm going by train.

mistake.display: Dado no tengo tiempo, hoy como en casa.
mistake.why: The que belongs to the connector. Without it, dado is just a past participle.

sentences.usage: Written Spanish, or a considered spoken explanation. Neutral, and a friend would hear ya que instead.
sentences.mnemonic: All three front-loaders end in que, and none of them may drop it.

sentences.display: Hay obras en la calle; sin embargo, no hay mucho ruido.
sentences.cue: There are roadworks in the street; even so, there isn't much noise.

words.note: Indexed whole, because bare sin is a different word. It opens the clause that CONTRADICTS what came before — the mirror of por eso, which opens the clause that follows from it.

sentences.trap: sin embargo is however, not nevertheless-and-therefore: it cancels the expectation the first clause raised. English however can also mean in whatever way; Spanish sin embargo never does.
sentences.sound: sin em-BAR-go, stress on the bar, and the phrase is always followed by a comma.

variations.display: Hay huelga; sin embargo, hay tren.
variations.cue: There's a strike; even so, there's a train.
variations.changed: the cause and what survives it

variations.display: Llueve mucho; sin embargo, vamos en coche.
variations.cue: It's raining hard; even so, we're going by car.

mistake.display: Sin embargo hay obras, no hay mucho ruido.
mistake.why: sin embargo opens the surprising half, not the expected one. The roadworks are the fact; the quiet is the surprise.

sentences.usage: Written or careful Spanish. Neutral, and pero is what the same thought sounds like out loud.
sentences.mnemonic: sin embargo cancels; por eso confirms.

sentences.display: No hay tren y hay huelga; por lo tanto, hoy no salimos.
sentences.cue: There's no train and there's a strike; therefore we're not going out today.

words.note: Three tokens, indexed whole. The formal twin of así que and por eso: same position, after the cause, and a register a conversation rarely reaches for.

sentences.trap: English therefore is stiff and Spanish por lo tanto is stiff in exactly the same way, so the register maps for once. What does not map is the position: it is fixed after the cause, where English can also say we therefore.
sentences.sound: por lo TAN-to, three words run as one phrase, stress on the tan.

variations.display: Hay obras y hay huelga; por lo tanto, no hay autobús.
variations.cue: There are roadworks and a strike; therefore there's no bus.

variations.display: No tengo tiempo; por lo tanto, hoy como en casa.
variations.cue: I don't have time; therefore I'm eating at home today.

mistake.display: Por lo tanto no hay tren, no salimos.
mistake.why: por lo tanto opens the consequence. In front of the cause it claims the missing train is the result.

sentences.usage: A notice, a report, or someone being deliberately precise. Neutral leaning formal; the spoken version of this whole line is así que.
sentences.mnemonic: Two causes stacked, one por lo tanto to close them.
